newsitem.title: UK: Britain plays down St Helena rebellion reports.
newsitem.headline: Britain plays down St Helena rebellion reports.

text.p: Britain on Tuesday played down reports of riots and rising tension on the tiny Atlantic dependency of St Helena, saying there was no orchestrated uprising there.

An official on the remote island, most famous as Napoleon's place of exile after his defeat at the battle of Waterloo, said two of the ruling council's five members resigned last week, and a police van and a bus were set on fire at the start of April.

"We are aware of the unfortunate incidents and attacks on property...on April 2. We have no evidence that these are linked to anti-government sentiment or an orchestrated campaign," a Foreign Office spokesman said.
The island's governor, David Smallman, has left the island for a spell of leave, but the Foreign Office said this was entirely coincidental.
"The governor's absence on mid-tour leave is wholly routine and was approved some weeks ago," the spokesman said. "There is no connection with recent events on the island."
A St Helena official said the resignations had created tension in the ruling council but elsewhere on the island the atmosphere was no worse than usual. Elections are due to be held there on July 9.

"Events in the council have been quite serious and there is probably a lot of tension in council. But on the island it's no more tense than normal," the official told Reuters by telephone."We've had dissatisfied feelings on the island for a while now."

The official said there was no sign that the fire attacks on the island were a protest against the government. "I don't know if it was in protest at anything. A few people have been arrested. From what we gather it was a drink-related incident," the official said.
Sources on the island say the main complaint among the population of about 5,500 is unemployment. Some islanders say the level of unemployment is too high while unemployment benefits are too low.

Like its sister island of Tristan da Cunha and the colony of Hong Kong, St Helena has a "dependency" status which allows its inhabitants British passports but denies them the right to live and work in Britain.

Britain says it is sympathetic to St Helena's problems but says it has been taking steps to bolster its economy and is supporting the island with a grant of 26 million pounds ($42.1 million) spread over three years. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
